metadata.title: How well does the digital home learning environment predict ICT literacy and ICT self-efficacy? Comparing the predictive power of adolescent and parent reports

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a convenience sample of 16 schools (33 grade 6 classes) in northern Germany, with students and parents linked via identification codes. The analysis is conducted in Mplus 8.4 using structural equation modeling with TYPE = COMPLEX to account for the nested classroom structure (class membership as the cluster variable), but the manuscript does not report the use of any ICILS/PISA-style sampling weights or replicate weights. Because no survey weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is mentioned, it is not possible to confirm population-representative weighting; the results should be interpreted as associations within this regional school sample. For analysts working with ILSA microdata, the appropriate approach would be to apply the official student sampling weights and replicate weights (if available) for variance estimation; however, this paper’s reported workflow does not document such weighting.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the outcomes are not ILSA PV-based achievement scores: ICT literacy is measured via an objective multiple-choice test (TILT-Grade 6) scored using weighted maximum likelihood estimates (WLE), and ICT self-efficacy is measured with a 4-point Likert-type scale. Missing data handling is described using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus, which is a model-based approach rather than a PV-combining procedure; therefore PV handling does not apply to this study’s dependent variables.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Convenience sample collected in 2019 from 16 schools in northern Germany (33 grade 6 classes). Students completed the ICT literacy test and student questionnaire at school; parents completed the digital HLE questionnaire at home. The analytic sample was restricted to complete parent-child dyads after removing cases with missing data on central constructs (including the ICT literacy test and the digital HLE questionnaire), resulting in 422 complete dyads (from 553 students and 449 parents). Missingness on study variables was low overall (<2% per variable) except for parental ICT values (9.0%) and monitoring/supervision (6.9%), which were handled using FIML in Mplus.

main_findings.dataset_used: TILT-Grade 6 ICT literacy test (Germany, grade 6; 2019 data collection)
main_findings.performance_metrics: M1 (adolescent reports): R2 Total = 0.39; R2 Control variables = 0.12; ΔR2 Digital HLE = 0.27. Significant predictors: Parental ICT values (A) β = 0.32*; Monitoring/supervision (A) β = −0.40***. M2 (parent reports): R2 Total = 0.21; R2 Control variables = 0.12; ΔR2 Digital HLE = 0.09. Significant predictor: Monitoring/supervision (P) β = −0.24*. M3 (both perspectives): ICT self-efficacy exclusively predicted by adolescent reports with β in range |0.37|–|0.41|; R2 Total = 0.39; ΔR2 Digital HLE = 0.27.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TILT-Grade 6 ICT literacy test (Germany, grade 6; 2019 data collection) the study leveraged Parental ICT values and Monitoring/supervision (plus controls Gender and Educational level) to predict ICT self-efficacy, finding that adolescent-reported Parental ICT values positively predicted self-efficacy (β = 0.32) while adolescent-reported Monitoring/supervision negatively predicted it (β = −0.40), with substantial incremental explained variance (ΔR2 = 0.27). This indicates that strengthening autonomy-supportive parental beliefs about ICT and reducing controlling monitoring behaviors may improve adolescents’ ICT self-efficacy, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: TILT-Grade 6 ICT literacy test (Germany, grade 6; 2019 data collection)
main_findings.performance_metrics: M1 (adolescent reports): R2 Total = 0.24; R2 Control variables = 0.16; ΔR2 Digital HLE = 0.08. Significant predictors: Parental ICT values (A) β = 0.25*; Monitoring/supervision (A) β = −0.26*. M2 (parent reports): R2 Total = 0.34; R2 Control variables = 0.16; ΔR2 Digital HLE = 0.18. Significant predictors: Parental ICT values (P) β = 0.38***; Instructional support (P) β = 0.20*; Monitoring/supervision (P) β = −0.17*; Psychological support (P) β = −0.23* (suppression); Rules (P) β = −0.10 (ns). M2a (without psychological support): R2 = 0.31 vs. 0.35 with psychological support included. M3 (both perspectives): ICT literacy predicted only by parent reports with significant β in range |0.17|–|0.36|; R2 Total = 0.34; ΔR2 Digital HLE = 0.18.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TILT-Grade 6 ICT literacy test (Germany, grade 6; 2019 data collection) the study leveraged Parental ICT values, Monitoring/supervision, and (from parent reports) Instructional support and Psychological support to predict ICT literacy, finding that parent-reported Parental ICT values were the strongest positive predictor (β = 0.38***) while parent-reported Monitoring/supervision was a negative predictor (β = −0.17*), with larger incremental explained variance than adolescent reports (ΔR2 = 0.18 vs. 0.08). This indicates that interventions aiming to improve adolescents’ ICT skills should prioritize parents’ ICT-related beliefs and reduce controlling supervision, while also recognizing that psychological encouragement may function as a suppressor rather than a straightforward positive driver.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses a German grade-6 convenience sample (422 complete parent–child dyads from 16 schools in northern Germany; 2019) to examine whether a digital home learning environment (HLE) predicts two outcomes: ICT literacy (TILT-Grade 6 objective test scored with WLE) and ICT self-efficacy (10-item 4-point scale). The authors estimate predictive validity using Mplus regression/correlation models with controls for gender and educational level and account for classroom nesting via TYPE = COMPLEX. For ICT self-efficacy, adolescent reports of parental ICT values and monitoring/supervision show the strongest effects (ΔR2 = 0.27; β = 0.32* for values and β = −0.40*** for monitoring in M1), whereas parent reports add little (ΔR2 = 0.09). For ICT literacy, parent reports are more predictive (ΔR2 = 0.18), with parental ICT values as the strongest positive predictor (β = 0.38***) and monitoring/supervision as a negative predictor (β = −0.17*), while psychological support shows suppression effects. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (associations, not causal mechanisms) and the absence of documented survey-weighting for population generalization.
